article_title: Tapping Data for Frontline Talent Development
citation: Patti Constantakis and Sierra Noakes. (2019). Tapping Data for Frontline Talent Development. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: From a disconnected learning ecosystem to a worker-centered ecosystem
description: The report frames a transition model from a 'Disconnected Learning Ecosystem' — silos, insufficient analysis, data not in workers' hands — to a 'Worker-Centered Ecosystem' where workers access their own data, providers deliver personalized services, employers improve talent pipelines, and funders make informed investment decisions. The mechanism is data sharing and interoperability: 'Access to the right data will equip frontline workers with the agency and knowledge to make informed decisions about their future and will equip stakeholders with information needed to deliver high-quality services.'
requirements: Data must flow between stakeholders and back to frontline workers, which current processes and systems 'do not support'
constraints: Progress depends on resolving legal, incentive, and technical challenges the report identifies
target_learners: frontline workers in retail, healthcare, food service, and hospitality
target_learning_goals: career advancement and informed decisions about professional development
examples: The report contrasts a 'Here' state of disconnected silos with a 'There' state where workers can access their data to inform their decisions.
key_sources: Patti Constantakis and Sierra Noakes. (2019). Tapping Data for Frontline Talent Development. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/44b193d2-b037-4ded-8322-61e8fb00f89b

article_title: Tapping Data for Frontline Talent Development
citation: Patti Constantakis and Sierra Noakes. (2019). Tapping Data for Frontline Talent Development. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Give frontline workers access to their own skills and learning data so they can make informed career decisions
description: The report's core design principle is worker data agency: frontline workers 'likely do not have access to data regarding their own skills and learning and do not know what skills employers seek in quality workers'. Returning data to workers 'would help inform frontline workers' decisions around professional and career aspirations' and is the defining feature of the worker-centered ecosystem the report advocates.
requirements: Systems that share data back with frontline workers rather than only collecting from them
constraints: Requires resolving privacy-regulation understanding, incentive gaps, and technical interoperability barriers
target_learners: frontline workers making less than $30K per year with job-limiting foundational skills
target_learning_goals: informed professional and career decisions, upskilling
examples: The report states data sharing will help improve programs and services, create more personalized interventions, and improve talent pipelines.
key_sources: Patti Constantakis and Sierra Noakes. (2019). Tapping Data for Frontline Talent Development. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/44b193d2-b037-4ded-8322-61e8fb00f89b

article_title: AI Literacy in the Workforce
citation: Zachariah, I., Dallas, D., Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., & Karim. (2025). AI literacy for the Workforce. In Ruiz, P. et al. (Eds.), Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/271
title: Workforce AI literacy framework of six skill and competency domains
description: The brief defines AI literacy as "a set of foundational skills and competencies that enable individuals to understand how AI works, responsibly evaluate AI systems, and use AI effectively as a human-centered tool across various contexts." Table 1 organizes workforce-specific AI skills into six domains: Technical Knowledge, Practical Implementation, Analytical Skills, Interpersonal and Communication Skills, Ethical Evaluation, and Adaptive Skills. The framework is adapted from National Academies, OECD, Learning Guild, World Economic Forum, Microsoft, and AI Education Project sources.
requirements: Workers need both technical AI competencies and enhanced human skills that complement AI capabilities
constraints: The specific technical knowledge, skills, and competencies needed for AI implementation vary significantly across sectors
target_learners: current and future workforce members across industries
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI systems function and their limitations
evaluating AI outputs and mitigating risks
examples: Table 2 illustrates sector examples in healthcare, finance, and creative fields, including an AI-powered wound assessment tool and AI-assisted restoration of The Night Watch
key_sources: Zachariah, I., Dallas, D., Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., & Karim. (2025). AI literacy for the Workforce. In Ruiz, P. et al. (Eds.), Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/271

article_title: Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment
citation: Dongming Mei, Katherine Moore, and Ben Sayler. (2026). Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09624
title: Workflow-aligned AI literacy framework for AI-powered materials discovery
description: The paper's central framework defines AI literacy for materials discovery as competency aligned to a closed-loop workflow of data, representation, modeling, and experiment, rather than generic tool fluency. It states that students 'should learn to explain where data came from, why a representation is physically meaningful, how a model was validated, what uncertainty remains, whether a prediction is experimentally plausible.' The framework integrates AI literacy, materials-informatics competency, and outcome-oriented equity, which the authors say are often treated separately.
requirements: Learning outcomes must be aligned with the end-to-end materials discovery loop, including data provenance, featurization, validation, uncertainty, and experimental feedback
constraints: The paper presents no new empirical data from an implemented curriculum; artifacts are 'adaptable templates rather than fixed prescriptions'
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate materials science students
examples: Figure 1 maps the closed loop connecting 'data provenance and quality, representation and featurization, modeling and validation, uncertainty-aware decision making, and experimental synthesis/testing'
key_sources: Dongming Mei, Katherine Moore, and Ben Sayler. (2026). Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09624

article_title: Through the WordStream Glass: Revisiting Quantitative Encoding for Qualitative Learning Analytics
citation: Huyen N. Nguyen, Kathleen A. Bowe, Minh-Huyen Nguyen, Kit Thompson, Caleb M. Trujillo. (2026). Through the WordStream Glass: Revisiting Quantitative Encoding for Qualitative Learning Analytics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18692
title: WordStream Maker: no-code end-to-end tool for authoring custom WordStream visualizations
description: WordStream Maker is a general-purpose, no-code, end-to-end tool for constructing WordStream visualizations, designed for users with little or no programming background. Its graphical interface accepts tabular text input and runs a single pipeline streamlining data wrangling, NLP, and visualization, with user-selectable display parameters including part-of-speech categories and scoring methods such as frequency, sudden attention, and TF–IDF. It produces aggregate visualizations from uploaded data at runtime without linked source text, supporting visualization creation.
requirements: Users with little or no programming background; tabular text input
constraints: No linked source text; limited to the tool's single pipeline rather than a fixed linked corpus
target_learners: Qualitative researchers and instructors without programming experience
target_learning_goals: Authoring custom visualizations of qualitative time-series text data
examples: Participants used the Maker on the same 62-student reflection corpus during the study tasks
key_sources: Huyen N. Nguyen, Kathleen A. Bowe, Minh-Huyen Nguyen, Kit Thompson, Caleb M. Trujillo. (2026). Through the WordStream Glass: Revisiting Quantitative Encoding for Qualitative Learning Analytics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18692

article_title: A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era
citation: Smith, Dalton Ross; Whittington, Wilburn; Martinez, Alejandro; Duncan, Aidan; Li, Gang. (2026). A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11540
title: Workforce Readiness Level (WRL): a nine-stage, TRL-like scale of individual manufacturing competency
description: The WRL is a ranked measure of an individual's demonstrated competency to perform, supervise, or improve manufacturing tasks, reported as an integer from 1 to 9. It adapts NASA's Technology Readiness Level structure to people: "structurally similar to NASA's Technology Readiness Level scale, that lays out progressive competency milestones for AI-era manufacturing". Stages group into awareness (1-3), applied practice (4-6), and autonomous leadership (7-9) bands, with stackable-credential articulation points at WRL 3, 5, and 7, and descriptors written as observable behaviors so two raters can score them.
requirements: Competency must be demonstrated through observable performance on artifacts, not coursework completion or self-report
Progression is stage-gated and monotonic, so downstream stakeholders can rely on the construct without re-arguing evidence
constraints: The nine-level count is inherited from TRL/MRL as a design choice, not derived from data; whether a coarser or finer partition fits competency growth is left open
The mechanism is domain-general; the AI-specific content lies in the pillar choice, and adaptation to low-AI settings is outside the paper's scope
target_learning_goals: AI-era smart-manufacturing competency from awareness through autonomous innovation leadership
examples: Programs publish example artifacts for each stage, such as a reference cobot-teaching pendant program for WRL 4, so raters and learners share a concrete target
key_sources: Smith, Dalton Ross; Whittington, Wilburn; Martinez, Alejandro; Duncan, Aidan; Li, Gang. (2026). A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11540

article_title: Learning from Examples: Instructional Principles from the Worked Examples Research
citation: Atkinson, R. K., Derry, S. J., Renkl, A., & Wortham, D. (2000). Learning from Examples: Instructional Principles from the Worked Examples Research. Review of Educational Research, 70(2), 181-214. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543070002181
title: A three-factor causal framework organizes the factors that influence learning from worked examples
description: The review proposes a framework representing a causal model of the major factors shown to influence learning from worked examples, which it defines as 'instructional devices that provide an expert's problem solution for a learner to study'. The framework groups moderators into 'intra-example features, in other words, how the example is designed', inter-example features concerning relationships among examples and practice problems within a lesson, and individual differences in how students self-explain examples.
requirements: Effective examples must have highly integrated components, employing multiple modalities in presentation and emphasizing conceptual structure by labeling or segmenting
Examples should be presented in close proximity to matched practice problems
constraints: Studying worked examples is not the preferred method when the instructional goal is the third stage of skill acquisition, automatic performance, where problem-solving practice is of critical importance
target_learners: novices in domains such as mathematics, physics, and computer programming
examples: The review derives the framework from laboratory experiments and classroom investigations across mathematics, physics, and computer programming, deliberately drawing on multiple research groups and theoretical viewpoints rather than one research program
key_sources: Atkinson, R. K., Derry, S. J., Renkl, A., & Wortham, D. (2000). Learning from Examples: Instructional Principles from the Worked Examples Research. Review of Educational Research, 70(2), 181-214. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543070002181

article_title: Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect
citation: Leppink, J., Broers, N. J., Imbos, T., van der Vleuten, C. P. M., & Berger, M. P. F. (2012). Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect. Higher Education, 63, 771-785. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-011-9476-1
title: Introduce new subject matter with worked-out examples, then shift students to formulating arguments once they have sufficient prior knowledge
description: The article's recommendation for teaching practice is sequential: "Confronting students with worked-out examples of arguments appears to be a good initiative for teachers introducing the subject matter to be learned, and for elaborating on students' limited prior knowledge." Once students have sufficient prior knowledge, knowledge elaboration by means of argumentation imposes germane load and improves conceptual understanding. Matching the instructional method to the learner's current prior knowledge avoids the expertise reversal effect the experiment demonstrated.
requirements: Some assessment of students' current prior knowledge is needed to decide when to switch from studying worked-out examples to self-generated argumentation
constraints: Argumentation on flawed or incomplete knowledge imposes extraneous load and can worsen low prior knowledge students' conceptual understanding below that of merely reading the text
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of the sampling distribution of the mean
examples: The experiment compared worked-out examples of arguments (Box 3) against self-formulated arguments (Box 2) within a 60-minute study session, keeping time-on-task constant across conditions
key_sources: Leppink, J., Broers, N. J., Imbos, T., van der Vleuten, C. P. M., & Berger, M. P. F. (2012). Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect. Higher Education, 63, 771-785. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-011-9476-1

article_title: Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive #x0022;Quantified Self #x0022;
citation: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf
title: Wordometer app for the SMI iView X eye tracker
description: The Wordometer is a prototype application created for the SMI iView X eye tracker that "estimates the number of words a person reads, much like a pedometer counts steps". It works by detecting line breaks from long saccades against the reading direction and feeding them, with eye-gaze features, into a support vector regression algorithm. The article presents it as a reading-habits quantification tool analogous to fitness trackers.
requirements: Requires a mobile eye tracker (the SMI iView X) recording eye gaze while the user reads
constraints: Evaluated only with users reading English documents
target_learning_goals: quantifying reading volume as a measure of mental fitness
examples: The authors recorded eye movements of numerous users reading English documents and applied a line-break detector before training the word-count estimator
key_sources: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf

article_title: When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents’ world knowledge-based audience design
citation: Arvidsson C., Pagmar D., Uddén J. (2022). When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents' world knowledge-based audience design. Royal Society Open Science 9(11): 220305. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.220305
title: Novel world knowledge-based audience design task with post-test knowledge attribution survey
description: A modified director task measuring adaptation to addressees' world knowledge rather than visual perspective. In each trial a pictured addressee (a child or an elderly woman) appears while the speaker records a message about a target referent; "the participant knew the name of the target referent but was expected to assume that the addressee either (i) did not know the name of the target (unknown test condition) or (ii) did know the name of the target (known control condition)". A post-test survey controls for assumed knowledge, yielding a knowledge attribution score, and the AD score subtracts redundant describing in the known condition from sufficient describing in the unknown condition.
requirements: Participants must know the names of target referents and hold condition-matching assumptions, verified by the post-test survey; stimuli require no more than one modifier for an unambiguous description
constraints: Conducted with passive confederates, which the authors note have been criticized since interactive contexts increase speakers' informativeness; individual language ability was not included as a model variable
examples: 36 trials (24 unknown, 12 known) implemented in PsychoPy; the practice trial was always a known-condition trial to prevent participants from adopting constant describing
key_sources: Arvidsson C., Pagmar D., Uddén J. (2022). When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents' world knowledge-based audience design. Royal Society Open Science 9(11): 220305. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.220305

article_title: Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education
citation: Cowan Nelson. (2014). Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4207727/
title: Working memory as the small amount of information held in an especially accessible state for use in cognitive tasks
description: The article defines working memory as "the small amount of information that can be held in an especially accessible state and used in cognitive tasks," contrasting it with the vast store of long-term memory. It traces the concept from Locke, James, and Miller through Broadbent, Baddeley and Hitch, and Cowan's own embedded-processes model, in which a subset of activated long-term memory lies in the focus of attention. The framework underpins the article's claims about development, learning, and education.
requirements: Working memory must be distinguished from long-term memory, with the focus of attention holding only a few integrated items or chunks within activated long-term memory
constraints: The article notes the reason for the capacity limit is unknown, with biological, evolutionary, and teleological accounts still under debate
target_learners: learners from infancy to old age
examples: The article uses the example of holding the notion of a cat and the notion of stripes at the same time to grasp the tiger concept correctly
key_sources: Cowan Nelson. (2014). Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4207727/

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Integrating cognitive load and social-cognitive research perspectives on example-based learning (worked examples vs. modeling examples)
description: The special issue's third article (Van Gog & Rummel) reviews and contrasts two example-based learning traditions: worked examples, studied in cognitive load research as didactical worked-out problem solutions in written format, and modeling examples, studied in social-cognitive research where learners observe someone performing a task. The article argues the two forms have "clear and interesting connections and analogs" and that studies drawing on both perspectives may advance the knowledge base on example-based learning.
requirements: Researchers must consider measures from both traditions, e.g., cognitive load in modeling-example studies and self-efficacy in worked-example studies
constraints: Model characteristics such as age, gender, and type of performance are not relevant for written worked examples but may matter in video-based examples or animations
target_learners: learners studying worked or modeled problem solutions
examples: Modeling-example research considers model characteristics such as mastery vs. coping type of performance
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Differences between presentation methods in working memory procedures: A matter of working memory consolidation.
citation: Ricker Timothy J., Cowan Nelson. (2014). Differences between Presentation Methods in Working Memory Procedures: A Matter of Working Memory Consolidation. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034301
title: Working memory consolidation account of time-based forgetting
description: The article proposes that a post-encoding consolidation process, continuing after pattern masking, strengthens working memory traces and determines their vulnerability to time-based forgetting. Consolidation is distinguished from encoding: "consolidation is further processing that can occur even after a mask, and that helps makes the representation of the stimulus more resistant to forgetting". The experiments show that "the total amount of time available to consolidate the stimuli into working memory is what is important", reconciling studies that do and do not find duration-based forgetting. Candidate mechanisms discussed include attentional refreshing, neural desynchronization, and pattern identification or chunking.
requirements: Requires an encoded memory trace and central resources for consolidation to proceed after masking, as suggested by Jolicoeur and Dell'Acqua (1998)
constraints: The finding was obtained always with fairly substantial encoding times of at least 250 ms per item
The article does not try to distinguish short-term consolidation empirically from long-term consolidation, calling this a major and difficult future issue
The study did not manipulate interference, so consolidation's effect on interference-based forgetting is speculative
target_learners: adult college students performing working memory tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding maintenance of information in working memory over short retention intervals
examples: Across the four experiments, sequential conditions with post-mask free time showed 0.19-0.22 items forgotten between 1 and 12 s, while conditions without such free time showed 0.39-0.67 items forgotten.
key_sources: Ricker Timothy J., Cowan Nelson. (2014). Differences between Presentation Methods in Working Memory Procedures: A Matter of Working Memory Consolidation. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034301

article_title: Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data
citation: Liang, C., Toyokawa, Y., & Ogata, H. (2025). Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09452-9
title: Group formation system with automatic grouping panel, group composition visualization, and Wordcloud group-awareness tool
description: A group formation system embedded in the LEAF infrastructure that automates grouping from learning log data. Teachers configure groups through an automatic grouping panel with pre-configured inputs, view each group's input characteristics via colored bar graphs in a group composition panel, and monitor performance through an evaluation panel for formative feedback. A Wordcloud visualization module acts as a GAT for active reading, displaying key terms highlighted by group members in BookRoll so that, for example, a word "appears prominently among other red markers in the Wordcloud, indicating frequent highlights by multiple group members", supporting discussion initiation and peer learning while preserving privacy by not naming individual proficiency.
requirements: LEAF infrastructure consolidating LMS and BookRoll xAPI interaction logs; marker data collected during an individual active reading phase before grouping
constraints: Logs must be cleaned of duplicated markers in the same area and markers on irrelevant pages, which the authors note calls for context-based data-cleaning methods
Wordcloud comparisons between Used and Non-used students were exploratory post-hoc subgroup analyses
target_learners: Senior high school EFL students and their classroom teacher
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary learning, text comprehension, and group knowledge awareness in collaborative active reading
examples: In the empirical study the system formed 10 four-student groups per condition, presenting Wordclouds derived from each group's marker matrix during the group learning phase
key_sources: Liang, C., Toyokawa, Y., & Ogata, H. (2025). Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09452-9

article_title: How preparation-for-learning with a worked versus an open inventing problem affect subsequent learning processes in pre-service teachers
citation: Inga Glogger-Frey, Anne-Katrin Treier, Alexander Renkl. (2022). How preparation-for-learning with a worked versus an open inventing problem affect subsequent learning processes in pre-service teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09577-6
title: Use worked-example preparation rather than open inventing to prepare learners for subsequent instruction in complex, ill-structured domains
description: The article argues that when learning content has high element interactivity, preparing learners by having them study a worked-out solution of the invention problem deepens and focuses the subsequent learning phase. It concludes that "working through a worked example deepens future learning and thus is more beneficial for transfer than preparation with an open inventing problem" in comparable learning domains. The mechanism is more elaboration and more application of canonical criteria during future learning.
requirements: Learners with low prior knowledge facing complex learning contents, for whom direct guidance to canonical solutions and key concepts is argued to save time and cognitive resources
constraints: The authors state generalizations can be limited: effects may depend on learner expertise and element interactivity, and the opposite effect (inventing > worked example) was found when school students gained expertise through practice; only an immediate posttest was used
target_learners: novice learners with low prior knowledge in complex domains
target_learning_goals: assessing the quality of learning strategies
applying quality criteria to new instances
examples: In the experiment, the inventing group generated evaluation criteria from four contrasting learning-journal extracts while the worked-example group studied the same extracts with the criteria, ratings and notes already filled in by an experienced teacher, both for 15 minutes before learning in the CBLE
key_sources: Inga Glogger-Frey, Anne-Katrin Treier, Alexander Renkl. (2022). How preparation-for-learning with a worked versus an open inventing problem affect subsequent learning processes in pre-service teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09577-6

article_title: Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning
citation: Hanna Grimm · Peter A. Edelsbrunner · Kornelia Möller. (2023). Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09601-9
title: Wooden sorting box as a static structuring scaffold for modeling hypothesis-based reasoning
description: A wooden sorting box used by teachers and student pairs to structure and visualize the conditional reasoning process: objects fulfilling the premise are tested, and outcomes are sorted into fields marked by a green smiley (verifies), a red smiley (refutes), or a yellow smiley (premise not fulfilled, no information). The article states "the wooden sorting box was aimed at helping the students to structure and visualize the complex hypothesis-based reasoning process (structuring scaffolds)" and that it was intended to relieve working memory by reducing cognitive load and supporting inhibition of irrelevant information.
requirements: Teachers received three three-hour training courses plus detailed teaching scripts and materials to implement the box and the accompanying cognitively activating questions
constraints: The box served as a static scaffold (not individually adaptive); adaptivity came from the teacher's verbal scaffolds during inquiry
target_learners: third-grade elementary students in whole science classes
target_learning_goals: hypothesis-based reasoning with conditionals: distinguishing relevant from irrelevant events and affirmative from refuting outcomes
examples: The teacher modeled the process with a table tennis ball under the hypothesis 'objects that are filled with air bounce', then pairs used one sorting box each while the teacher posed structuring and problematizing questions adaptively, fading support
key_sources: Hanna Grimm · Peter A. Edelsbrunner · Kornelia Möller. (2023). Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09601-9

article_title: Confidence in COVID problem solving: What factors predict adults’ item-level metacognitive judgments on health-related math problems before and after an educational intervention?
citation: Scheibe, D. A., Fitzsimmons, C. J., Mielicki, M. K., Taber, J. M., Sidney, P. G., Coifman, K., & Thompson, C. A. (2022). Confidence in COVID problem solving: What factors predict adults’ item-level metacognitive judgments on health-related math problems before and after an educational intervention? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09300-3
title: Worked-example educational intervention with apple-orchard analogy for case-fatality-rate problems
description: The intervention was a step-by-step worked example designed to combat whole number bias in ratio comparison. It used "an analogy to a familiar context–an apple orchard" illustrating procedural steps for calculating a case-fatality rate, emphasizing number lines and relational reasoning, then asked participants to map the analogy to a health-context worked example comparing COVID-19 and flu case-fatality rates. In the parent study it improved problem-solving accuracy relative to business-as-usual control, and in this analysis it raised monitoring judgments.
requirements: Participants must engage with the worked example before solving target problems; the parent study randomly assigned participants to intervention or business-as-usual control
constraints: The intervention did not include feedback or practice problems, which the authors note may artificially increase monitoring judgments without improving monitoring accuracy
target_learners: adults in a Qualtrics panel solving health statistics problems
target_learning_goals: correct comparison of case-fatality and infection rates (rational-number reasoning)
examples: Participants saw an apple-orchard worked example, drew an analogy to a health worked example, then solved three posttest problems with strategy reports and confidence sliders
key_sources: Scheibe, D. A., Fitzsimmons, C. J., Mielicki, M. K., Taber, J. M., Sidney, P. G., Coifman, K., & Thompson, C. A. (2022). Confidence in COVID problem solving: What factors predict adults’ item-level metacognitive judgments on health-related math problems before and after an educational intervention? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09300-3

article_title: World Bank Influence on Policy Formation in Education: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Edwards Jr., D. Brent; Caravaca Hernández, Alejandro; Rappeport, Annie; et al. (2023). World Bank influence on policy formation in education: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, Vol. 94, Núm. 4. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231194725
title: Eleven-pathway typology of World Bank influence on national education policy formation
description: The review proposes a typology of 11 'pathways' of World Bank influence, defined as 'those observable avenues through which the World Bank exercises its influence (Samoff, 2009)'. The framework draws on the work of Roger Dale and Joel Samoff on forms of influence of international organizations, combining, retaining and separating pathways relevant to the World Bank. The pathways range from issuing loans to producing research, offering technical assistance, and guiding the work and investments of other international organizations, and each is illustrated with examples from the retained literature.
requirements: Studies must shed light on World Bank involvement and influence in policymaking processes at the national level, where policy means decisions taken by political actors on behalf of the state
constraints: The review is not exhaustive of all World Bank literature; it covers studies providing insight on policy formation rather than the effects of World Bank projects in practice, and books were not included
target_learners: Education policymakers and researchers studying international organizations in education
target_learning_goals: Understanding the specific avenues through which international organizations influence national education policy formation
examples: The review's results section discusses each pathway in turn, including loans, conditionalities, pilot projects, and technical assistance, with country examples such as Nepal, Tanzania, Egypt, El Salvador, and China
key_sources: Edwards Jr., D. Brent; Caravaca Hernández, Alejandro; Rappeport, Annie; et al. (2023). World Bank influence on policy formation in education: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, Vol. 94, Núm. 4. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231194725

article_title: Eye-Tracking in Educational Practice: Investigating Visual Perception Underlying Teaching and Learning in the Classroom
citation: Jarodzka, H., Skuballa, I., & Gruber, H. (2020). Eye-Tracking in Educational Practice: Investigating Visual Perception Underlying Teaching and Learning in the Classroom. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09565-7
title: Wolff, Jarodzka, and Boshuizen's model of teachers' classroom management scripts linking knowledge, perception, and situational awareness
description: The article presents the first detailed theoretical framework for research on teachers' professional vision: a model of teachers' classroom management scripts incorporating organized knowledge and perception with their effects on situational awareness and representations of classroom events, developed by contrasting novice and expert teachers. The review states this model "can not only help to synergize existing research into a broader picture but also clearly point towards new research avenues." It is expected to enable a shift from exploration to hypothesis-driven research.
requirements: Future empirical research to test and improve the model, moving beyond mere explorations
constraints: The field previously lacked specific theoretical models of cognitive and perceptual processes underlying teachers' classroom behavior and had to borrow from adjacent fields, which did not allow for specific predictions
target_learning_goals: understanding how teachers' knowledge and visual perception support classroom management and situational awareness
examples: The model contrasts novice and expert teachers' organized knowledge, perception, situational awareness, and representations of classroom events
key_sources: Jarodzka, H., Skuballa, I., & Gruber, H. (2020). Eye-Tracking in Educational Practice: Investigating Visual Perception Underlying Teaching and Learning in the Classroom. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09565-7

article_title: The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving
citation: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235
title: Four-type taxonomy of word-problem process models by process order and mental representation
description: The article organizes existing cognitive models of word-problem solving along two axes: whether text comprehension and computation occur in a "linear" or "flexible" order, and whether they use "separable or integrated mental representations". This yields four model types (linear-separable, flexible-separable, linear-integrated, flexible-integrated), each predicting distinct patterns of canonical, phase-crossover, and attention-crossover effects on eye-tracking data. The taxonomy is used to judge which model best fits the observed solution process.
requirements: Requires process data (e.g., eye-tracking) that distinguishes solution phases and areas of interest to discriminate between model types
constraints: The direct translation strategy is excluded from the taxonomy because it is "generally unreliable" and expected mostly in low-achieving solvers
target_learning_goals: understanding the cognitive process of mathematical word-problem solving
key_sources: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235

article_title: Training children’s spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding
citation: Nadja Lindner, Korbinian Moeller, Frauke Hildebrandt, Marcus Hasselhorn, Jan Lonnemann. (2025). Training children's spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102191. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102191
title: Working-memory serial-order and symbolic-representation alternative explanations
description: The article presents two alternative mechanisms attributed to Georges et al. (2023) and Gilligan-Lee et al. (2021). One holds that mastery of spatial terms may facilitate "the spatialization of ordered sequences in working memory and/or spatial attentional scanning processes". The other holds that spatial terms and symbolic numbers both require associating verbal labels with concepts, so spatial language training may have facilitated symbolic number representations. The authors state their design cannot decide between these accounts.
requirements: Further studies, e.g. training spatial language from another category not expected to facilitate numerical processing, to evaluate the symbolic-representation account
constraints: The study design does not allow deciding whether the effect is based on working-memory serial-order mapping, long-term-memory magnitude mapping, or both
examples: The authors note some children produced above/below instead of behind/in front of, suggesting vertical as well as sagittal and horizontal dimensions may be associated with numerical magnitudes
key_sources: Nadja Lindner, Korbinian Moeller, Frauke Hildebrandt, Marcus Hasselhorn, Jan Lonnemann. (2025). Training children's spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102191. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102191

article_title: Aphasic performance in the Terman Vocabulary Test.
citation: Wells, F. L. (1922). Aphasic performance in the Terman vocabulary test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072510
title: Word knowledge splits into ability to use/complete a word versus ability to define it by relation to other words
description: The article proposes that vocabulary testing taps two separable abilities: the ability to complete and use a word, and the ability to relate it to the words that describe it. As the author puts it, "Defining a word is not a test of 'knowing' the word itself, but of knowing its relation to certain other words that describe it." In the aphasic case, combination remained relatively intact while definitional association was disturbed; the author also notes people use function words they cannot define, and that some words are more fairly tested one way than the other.
requirements: A test of definitional knowledge presumes intact association between the word and the words that describe its meaning; this association is what aphasic word-amnesia disturbs
constraints: Derived from a single aphasic case; the author cautions some words are more fairly tested by combination, others by definition
target_learners: patients with aphasia or word-finding difficulty
examples: The patient answered definition items with fragmentary or insufficient responses (e.g. impolite, quake, plumbing) that the author calls fair examples of word-amnesia, while completing the same words in context
key_sources: Wells, F. L. (1922). Aphasic performance in the Terman vocabulary test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072510

article_title: A new scale of mental and physical measurements for adolescents and some of its uses.
citation: Woolley, Helen Thompson. (1915). A new scale of mental and physical measurements for adolescents, and some of its uses. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(9), 521-550.
title: A composite adolescent measurement scale built from averaged ten-percentile ranks on mental and physical tests
description: The scale ranks each child from one to ten on every mental and physical test according to the percentile in which the result falls, averages these ranks separately for physical measures (excluding height and weight) and mental measures, and places the average on general ten-percentile tables normed separately by sex and age. It was based on 750 fourteen-year-old children dropping out of school to work and 680 of the same children at fifteen, and places each individual 'in comparison with a large group of supposedly normal people of his own age and sex'. The article calls it 'a first attempt to formulate this kind of a standard, and is very rough in form'.
requirements: Requires giving the child the same series of tests on which the percentile tables are based and ranking each result by the printed percentile tables for the child's age and sex
constraints: Norms apply to fourteen and fifteen year old native born white working children; school-child scales were not yet published
The authors call the method 'a very rough one' and suggest increasing the number, variety and difficulty of tests and finer divisions
target_learners: fourteen and fifteen year old working children (native born white)
target_learning_goals: assessment of native mental and physical endowment for educational and vocational guidance
examples: Percentile tables for vital capacity, grip, steadiness, tapping, fatigue index, card sorting, cancellation, memory, substitution, sentence completion, opposites, and puzzle boxes are appended for ages fourteen and fifteen
key_sources: Woolley, Helen Thompson. (1915). A new scale of mental and physical measurements for adolescents, and some of its uses. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(9), 521-550. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075644

article_title: The impacts of a high-school art-based program on academic achievements, creativity, and creative behaviors
citation: Pablo Egana-delSol. (2023). The impacts of a high-school art-based program on academic achievements, creativity, and creative behaviors. npj Science of Learning 8:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00187-6
title: School art programs should employ working artists rather than art teachers as workshop instructors
description: The article identifies the AP's distinguishing design feature as its use of "working artists as opposed to art teachers" in school workshops. Artists are "selected through an open competition" and "paid competitively," with the implementing partner's reputation and attractive salaries cited as explaining the capacity to "attract excellent artists to the program." This design choice is presented as the key novelty distinguishing the AP from traditional public school art education.
requirements: Competitive salaries to attract high-quality artists
Open competition selection process for artists
Implementing partner with sufficient reputation to attract excellent artists
target_learners: high school students in public schools
examples: The AP selected professional artists through open competition under guidance of BYAF, paying competitively to teach 90-min weekly semester-long workshops in public schools
key_sources: Pablo Egana-delSol. (2023). The impacts of a high-school art-based program on academic achievements, creativity, and creative behaviors. npj Science of Learning 8:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00187-6

article_title: Speech connectedness predicts reading performance three months in advance: a longitudinal experiment
citation: Bárbara Malcorra, Marina Ribeiro, Giovanna Jensen, Tamara Meletti & Natália Bezerra Mota. (2024). Speech connectedness predicts reading performance three months in advance: a longitudinal experiment. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00248-4
title: Word-recurrence graph analysis of oral narratives as a measure of speech connectedness
description: The article represents transcribed oral narratives as directed graphs in which "each node represents a word, and each directed edge represents the temporal order of consecutive words." Three connectedness attributes are computed: repeated edges (RE), largest connected component (LCC), and largest strongly connected component (LSC), using a 30-word moving window to control verbosity. The graphs "are not based on meaning but on recurrence patterns," which the authors argue lets them "reveal patterns of connectedness from the earliest stages of language acquisition because they do not rely on meaning or linguistic rules." Developmentally, RE decreases while LCC and LSC increase as children advance in schooling.
requirements: Audio-recorded, transcribed oral narratives (three 30-second narratives per session, concatenated)
constraints: Metrics reflect word recurrence patterns rather than semantic content or linguistic relationships
target_learners: first- and second-grade elementary school children (ages 5–8)
examples: Three positive-affect IAPS images (a baby, a dog, a dessert) each viewed for 15 seconds, with narratives limited to 30 seconds and analyzed via a 30-word moving window
key_sources: Bárbara Malcorra, Marina Ribeiro, Giovanna Jensen, Tamara Meletti & Natália Bezerra Mota. (2024). Speech connectedness predicts reading performance three months in advance: a longitudinal experiment. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00248-4

article_title: Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor
citation: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371
title: Workspace-integrated, format-isomorphic hint placement to reduce help avoidance
description: This pattern delivers unsolicited help by embedding it inside the student's problem-solving workspace rather than in a separate message area. The article's rationale: "placing Assertions contiguously within the area of student attention would make unsolicited hints more noticeable," and formatting them like student-derived steps leverages visual expectation to speed interpretation. Persuasive labelling ("Subgoal", "Try to justify the added goal") frames the help as part of normal tutor workflow, circumventing autonomy preferences that drive help avoidance.
requirements: Hint content must be renderable in the same visual format as student-produced steps.
The learner's attention must be reliably focused on the workspace where the help appears.
constraints: The article argues the pattern applies where help and workspace are otherwise physically separated; Message-style hints in this study often went unnoticed, possibly due to change blindness.
Only studied with unsolicited next-step hints whose content is identical to the control's.
examples: Assertions added a cyan, question-marked 'Subgoal' node in the Deep Thought workspace; Messages appeared as text below the workspace after one minute of inactivity.
key_sources: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371
grain_size: interaction-level design pattern for intelligent tutoring interfaces

article_title: Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics
citation: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8
title: Dataset of 2568 education-category metacognition articles from Web of Science (2000–2023)
description: The study assembled a corpus for bibliometric and topic-modeling analysis by searching WoS with the terms "metacognition*" or "metacognitive*" or "meta-cognitive*" in title, abstract, or keywords, confined to the education category. Two subject matter experts screened 3,801 retrieved publications against inclusion criteria (explicit metacognition focus in education settings, empirical study), achieving an inter-rater reliability score of 96% on 200 randomly chosen articles, yielding 2,568 qualifying publications spanning 2000 to 2023.
requirements: Articles must explicitly mention metacognition or metacognitive components as research focus in education settings and be empirical studies
constraints: Restricted to English-language journal articles in the WoS education category
target_learning_goals: mapping the research landscape of metacognition in education
examples: Two experts independently assessed 200 randomly chosen articles, resulting in an inter-rater reliability score of 96%
key_sources: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8

article_title: Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them?
citation: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0
title: Corpus of 19 demonstrated learning objects rated on WoI dimensions
description: Participants presented 19 learning objects: "13 shared one each, while two shared three each." Table 2 categorizes them as videos, simulations, eLearning sites, graphics, and LMS assignments, rating each on agency, receptivity, freedom of action, pace/time, and attention demand. Coding allowed finer-grained distinctions, with some objects falling between levels (e.g., between middle and high), visualized along a continuum in Fig. 4.
requirements: Analysis excluded default features of the technology resources, focusing on "what the participants created and how they made their learning objects interactive"
constraints: Ratings rest on designers' self-reported descriptions of their objects rather than direct measurement of user interaction behavior
examples: Object 15, a course site designed as a game on an LMS, was rated high agency, low receptivity, high freedom of action, high pace, middle attention demand
key_sources: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0

article_title: Effects of Worksheets on Problem-Solving Skills: Meta-Analytic Studies
citation: Widodo, S. A., Wijayanti, A., Irfan, M., Pusporini, W., Mariah, M., & Rochmiyati, S. (2023). Effects of worksheets on problem-solving skills: Meta-analytic studies. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 9(1), 151-167. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.9.1.151
title: Worksheets as learning tools and media that guide students through tasks
description: A worksheet is defined in the article as "a guide for students to learn a concept so that they can solve a problem" and as a learning tool providing instructions on tasks a student needs to complete. Worksheets can serve as a primary learning resource alongside the teacher, become learning centers in the classroom, and function as learning media conveying information. They may contain material, summaries, and tasks such as sample questions or guided practice questions.
requirements: Worksheets must be prepared before learning to be used during teaching and learning activities in the classroom
examples: The analyzed studies used worksheets combined with approaches and models such as problem-based learning, guided inquiry, POGIL, discovery learning, and realistic mathematics teaching.
key_sources: Widodo, S. A., Wijayanti, A., Irfan, M., Pusporini, W., Mariah, M., & Rochmiyati, S. (2023). Effects of worksheets on problem-solving skills: Meta-analytic studies. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 9(1), 151-167. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.9.1.151

article_title: Educational Interventions for Medical Students in Chronic Wound Care-A Scoping Review.
citation: Reiter Manuel, Busch Dorothee, Erfurt‐Berge Cornelia. (2025). Educational Interventions for Medical Students in Chronic Wound Care—A Scoping Review. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.70760
title: Wound care content is adaptable across diverse educational settings and formats
description: The review's Table 4 summarises that "Wound care education can be integrated in different educational settings," including theoretical learning modules, practical skills training, skills labs, clinical clerkships or rotations, case-based training, simulation scenarios, and research-integrated curricula. Content can be taught standalone or embedded in superordinate curricula, in interprofessional learning groups, and focused on specific wounds or general wound care.
requirements: Depending on the educational setting, an orientation module or introduction to the topic is recommended, per the review's Table 4
constraints: None of the studies investigated whether differences in duration, attendance rules, assessment or media had an impact on participants' outcomes
target_learning_goals: chronic wound care knowledge and practical skills
examples: Included studies implemented wound care in clinical routine settings, during clerkships, and as standalone subjects or embedded within geriatrics curricula
key_sources: Reiter Manuel, Busch Dorothee, Erfurt‐Berge Cornelia. (2025). Educational Interventions for Medical Students in Chronic Wound Care—A Scoping Review. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.70760

article_title: The Implementation of Interactive Multimedia Learning Materials in Teaching Listening Skills
citation: Andi Tenri Ampa. (2015). The Implementation of Interactive Multimedia Learning Materials in Teaching Listening Skills. English Language Teaching, 8(12). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n12p56
title: Interactive multimedia listening materials built with Wondershare Quizcreator
description: The article's instructional component is a set of interactive multimedia materials for the university course 'listening skills', produced with the Wondershare Quizcreator program, consisting of "text and video of dialogue and monologue that are designed interactively with the users". The exercises include multiple choices, matching, filling the blanks, and true-false with answer keys, a time-limited quiz facility, instant review and feedback, and a self-grading system so students can check answers, find their scores, and repeat exercises. The materials were validated by experts and tried out with students before implementation.
requirements: Installation of a copy of the materials on every computer in the laboratory
Knowledge and skills in operating the computer, as the article cites Smith (2000) noting for preparing interactive multimedia
examples: Implemented with the experimental group for one-hour treatment meetings, while the control group received audio materials
key_sources: Andi Tenri Ampa. (2015). The Implementation of Interactive Multimedia Learning Materials in Teaching Listening Skills. English Language Teaching, 8(12). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n12p56

article_title: Vocabulary Learning through an Online Computerized Flashcard Site
citation: McLean, S., Hogg, N., & Rush, T. W. (2013). Vocabulary learning through an online computerized flashcard site. The JALT CALL Journal, 9(1), 79-98. https://jaltcall.org
title: Word Engine as an IRT/CAT-driven computerized flashcard program operationalizing paired-associate learning principles
description: Word Engine is a commercial online computerized flashcard site that operationalizes deliberate paired-associate vocabulary learning principles: retrieval practice, adaptive sequencing, expanded rehearsal, and generative use. It personalizes learning using measurement models: "Word Engine utilizes Item Response Theory (IRT) and Computer Adaptive Tests (CAT) when establishing a user’s vocabulary size, and IRT when selecting target items for learners." Its V-Check diagnostic assigns item difficulties and CAT selects items by response pattern. The authors chose it as the study's intervention partly because it provides a system for monitoring student use.
requirements: Learners must complete regular weekly sessions, since data from students who missed three or more consecutive weeks were excluded to preserve adaptive sequencing and expanded rehearsal
constraints: The program lacks productive recall and productive recognition tasks, and does not support users creating their own flashcards or automatic database support for entered words
target_learning_goals: receptive form-meaning knowledge of high-frequency English vocabulary
examples: Participants used the Basic course (most frequent 5000 words from Lexxica's corpus, including West's GSL and Coxhead's AWL) or the Advanced course, with words presented according to individual needs via IRT item selection
key_sources: McLean, S., Hogg, N., & Rush, T. W. (2013). Vocabulary learning through an online computerized flashcard site. The JALT CALL Journal, 9(1), 79-98. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1108008

article_title: Mobile Learning Based Worked Example in Electric Circuit (WEIEC) Application to Improve the High School Students' Electric Circuits Interpretation Ability
citation: Mitra Yadiannur and Supahar. (2017). Mobile Learning based Worked Example in Electric Circuit (WEIEC) Application to Improve the High School Students' Electric Circuits Interpretation Ability. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 12(3), 539-558.
title: Worked example effect as cognitive load reduction for problem solving
description: The article adopts the account that worked examples teach problem solving by presenting expert solutions with steps and final answers, and that their purpose "is to reduce the students' cognitive load when solving the problem". Conventional problem solving is said to raise excessive cognitive load unrelated to building problem solving ability, while learning from examples forms cognitive schemes reusable for other questions, especially benefiting students with low initial ability.
requirements: One worked example per learning session is insufficient to produce the worked example effect; students need follow-up questions with feedback, problems that encourage active processing, and learning of the consequences of each solution step
constraints: Presented as background theory from cited authors (Sweller, Renkl, Atkinson and others), not tested in this study
target_learners: high school physics students, particularly those with low initial ability
examples: The WEIEC application operationalises this sequence: principles/materials are presented, worked examples portray application, then evaluation and exam menus have students solve problems themselves
key_sources: Mitra Yadiannur and Supahar. (2017). Mobile Learning based Worked Example in Electric Circuit (WEIEC) Application to Improve the High School Students' Electric Circuits Interpretation Ability. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 12(3), 539-558. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1141565

article_title: Using Alice Software with 4C-ID Model: Effects in Programming Knowledge and Logical Reasoning
citation: Joana Martinho COSTA, Guilhermina Lobato MIRANDA. (2019). Using Alice Software with 4C-ID Model: Effects in Programming Knowledge and Logical Reasoning. Informatics in Education, 18(1), 1-15. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2019.01
title: Worksheet-driven problem sequence with just-in-time concepts and fading support
description: This instructional pattern sequences learning as worksheets, each describing a simulated problem to solve in Alice, with concepts introduced only when needed and teacher support progressively withdrawn. "Each worksheet had a few concepts which would only be approached in the moment in which they would be necessary to the resolution of the problem." After the first problems, "the students solved new problems in which they would have to use the previous concepts but relying on less support by the teacher", culminating in a challenge solved without any help. Students demonstrating autonomy were invited to explore other approaches, while others continued with heavy teacher support until prepared for the next problems.
requirements: The same teacher tutors the sequence and provides individualized cognitive and corrective feedback during worksheet resolution
target_learners: secondary vocational education students without prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: initial programming concepts such as variables, selection and repetition structures, sub-programming, and operations
examples: The ten-week program moved from software installation and adaptation, through five worksheets with weekly challenges, to a two-week free-theme short film project.
key_sources: Joana Martinho COSTA, Guilhermina Lobato MIRANDA. (2019). Using Alice Software with 4C-ID Model: Effects in Programming Knowledge and Logical Reasoning. Informatics in Education, 18(1), 1-15. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2019.01

article_title: Extended Discourse in First and Second Language Acquisition: A Challenge and an Opportunity
citation: Catherine E. Snow. (2014). Extended discourse in first and second language acquisition: A challenge and an opportunity! Journal of Japanese Linguistics 30. https://www.wordgen.serpmedia.org
title: Word Generation weekly unit pattern: debatable dilemma, embedded academic words, discussion activities, debate, and a taking-a-stand paragraph
description: A reusable lesson/unit pattern in which each week's dilemma is treated for 15-20 minutes a day over five days. Brief accessible articles present a balanced picture of a civic, moral, or economic dilemma with target academic words embedded; activities model additional word uses; a weekly debate lets students formulate and defend perspectives; and students write a brief paragraph arguing their own perspective using the target words. The article lists these as the program's basic design principles.
requirements: Topics must be of interest to students in the target age range
Articles must be brief and accessible and provide a balanced picture of the dilemma
Target words must be embedded in the articles and recur in varied contexts
constraints: Originally designed for 12-14 year old students in Boston Public Schools
Each dilemma is dealt with for 15-20 min a day for five days
target_learning_goals: formulating and defending perspectives in discussion
examples: In six Boston volunteer schools the pattern produced significant improvement on knowledge of the academic words taught; the article states students write "a brief 'taking a stand' paragraph, in which the students have the opportunity to argue for their own perspective and use the target words."
key_sources: Catherine E. Snow. (2014). Extended discourse in first and second language acquisition: A challenge and an opportunity! Journal of Japanese Linguistics 30. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED571513

article_title: Using Word Clouds in Online Discussions to Support Critical Thinking and Engagement
citation: deNoyelles, A., & Reyes-Foster, B. (2015). Using Word Clouds in Online Discussions to Support Critical Thinking and Engagement. Online Learning, 19(4). https://olj.onlinelearningconsortium.org/index.php/olj/article/view/478
title: Use word cloud analysis when open exploration matters more than correct answers
description: The article states that analyzing text in word cloud form is 'especially effective when the process is more important than right-or-wrong answers.' In the study, most students guessed the authors of the speeches incorrectly but still exhibited the critical thinking skills that can be generalized to other tasks. Word clouds also serve as a way to encourage open exploration of a concept without a large amount of text, and allow instructors to gauge students' prior and current knowledge.
requirements: The learning goal should emphasize analytical process over arriving at a correct answer
constraints: In the study most students guessed the speech authors incorrectly
examples: Students speculated about who wrote two famous speeches, at what point in history, and with what purpose, without needing to guess correctly
key_sources: deNoyelles, A., & Reyes-Foster, B. (2015). Using Word Clouds in Online Discussions to Support Critical Thinking and Engagement. Online Learning, 19(4). https://olj.onlinelearningconsortium.org/index.php/olj/article/view/478

article_title: Using Word Clouds in Online Discussions to Support Critical Thinking and Engagement
citation: deNoyelles, A., & Reyes-Foster, B. (2015). Using Word Clouds in Online Discussions to Support Critical Thinking and Engagement. Online Learning, 19(4). https://olj.onlinelearningconsortium.org/index.php/olj/article/view/478
title: Word cloud survey instrument measuring critical thinking, engagement, and peer interaction
description: The researchers developed an 18-item closed-ended survey with one open-ended item to measure student perceptions of critical thinking, engagement, and peer interaction after a word cloud or linear discussion activity. Items were generated from definitions and coding schemes employed in previous articles, and reliability was acceptable: Cronbach's alpha based on standardized items was .70 for the critical thinking scale and .84 for engagement. The instrument uses a 5-point Likert scale from agree to disagree.
requirements: Survey items were generated from the definitions and coding schemes employed in previous articles
constraints: The study approach is exploratory and results cannot generate strong generalizable results
examples: Sample items include 'This assignment challenged the way I think' and 'This assignment promoted interactions with my classmates'
key_sources: deNoyelles, A., & Reyes-Foster, B. (2015). Using Word Clouds in Online Discussions to Support Critical Thinking and Engagement. Online Learning, 19(4). https://olj.onlinelearningconsortium.org/index.php/olj/article/view/478

article_title: Increasing Reading Self-Efficacy and Reading Amount in EFL Learners with Word-Targets
citation: McLean, S., & Poulshock, J. (2018). Increasing reading self-efficacy and reading amount in EFL learners with word-targets. Reading in a Foreign Language, 30(1), 76–91. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Internalization of extrinsic motivation via word-targets (self-determination theory account)
description: The authors interpret their findings through Deci and Ryan's (1985) self-determination theory: word-target group participants 'experienced extrinsic motivation when they were required to read roughly double what they had previously read, and this extrinsic motivation was internalized and resulted in intrinsic motivation'. This internalization, plus a virtuous cycle of reading appropriate material (the extensive reading bootstrap hypothesis), explains why free reading and RSE continued to rise after targets were removed.
requirements: Targets must be attainable and set at appropriate material levels so learners experience success and enjoyment
constraints: The internalization account is the authors' interpretation supported by interviews and correlational evidence, not a direct test of the mechanism
examples: Participants reported finding longer books more interesting and continued choosing them after the 2,500-word target was removed
key_sources: McLean, S., & Poulshock, J. (2018). Increasing reading self-efficacy and reading amount in EFL learners with word-targets. Reading in a Foreign Language, 30(1), 76–91. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: The Impact of a Comparison Curriculum in Algebra I: A Randomized Experiment
citation: Star, J. R., Rittle-Johnson, B., Durkin, K., Newton, K., Pollack, C., Lynch, K., & Gogolen, C. (2013). The Impact of a Comparison Curriculum in Algebra I: A Randomized Experiment. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED000000
title: Infuse comparison into algebra teaching via side-by-side worked-example pairs with discussion questions
description: The intervention provided "a set of worked-example pairs, a presentation of two solved problems, placed side-by-side," each classified into one of four categories with a different instructional aim, with corresponding discussion questions and student worksheets. Approximately 150 pairs spanned first-year algebra topics. Teachers selected pairs fitting their course content and used them during class discussions of similarities and differences.
requirements: Teachers need professional development to learn about and practice using the materials (one-week 35-hour PD in the study)
constraints: Effects on student outcomes were negligible at the dosage and quality levels achieved in this trial
examples: Treatment teachers were instructed to use the materials at least two times per week for the 2010-2011 school year, selecting pairs that worked best with their course content
key_sources: Star, J. R., Rittle-Johnson, B., Durkin, K., Newton, K., Pollack, C., Lynch, K., & Gogolen, C. (2013). The Impact of a Comparison Curriculum in Algebra I: A Randomized Experiment. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED564086

article_title: A digital recipe for enhancing clinical reasoning: the role of e-learning by concordance (E-LbC): a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Aboueisha Hadeel, Abouzeid Enjy, Sallam Moataz A., Talaat Wagdy. (2025). A digital recipe for enhancing clinical reasoning: the role of e-learning by concordance (E-LbC): a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08005-w
title: Wooclap platform with integrated Script Concordance Test template
description: Wooclap is an interactive online platform used in this study to administer the SCT electronically and synchronously, letting students respond by mobile device, tablet, or computer with results displayed live on the teacher's screen. The article states: "Wooclap was selected due to its unique feature of having an integrated template for SCT (Script Concordance Test) within the system." It allowed tutors to collect, display, and compare student and expert answers on a single platform, providing automatic compilation of scores and immediate visualization of concordance levels between learners and experts.
requirements: Expert panel opinions must be gathered beforehand or collected within Wooclap before student responses can be compared to them
target_learning_goals: real-time classroom interaction and comprehension checking
examples: The pre- and post-SCT were conducted online, proctored and closed-book in the faculty electronic exam hall, with students completing the test individually within one and a half hours
key_sources: Aboueisha Hadeel, Abouzeid Enjy, Sallam Moataz A., Talaat Wagdy. (2025). A digital recipe for enhancing clinical reasoning: the role of e-learning by concordance (E-LbC): a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08005-w

article_title: Flipped classroom applied to Neurosurgery in undergraduate medical education.
citation: Gutiérrez-González R, Zamarron A, Royuela A, Rodriguez-Boto G. (2023). Flipped classroom applied to Neurosurgery in undergraduate medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04158-8
title: Wooclap gamification questionnaires as after-class review activities
description: Wooclap is an interactive electronic platform for creating polls and questionnaires answered anonymously through a device, self-paced or in real time. The authors designed nine questionnaires (averaging 7.4 questions each) to review the main concepts of each class; due to lack of time the activity was redesigned as self-paced after-class work. An average of 29 students (42.02% of those enrolled) participated per questionnaire, with an overall correct-answer rate of 52.7%. The authors valued it for feedback, detecting deficiencies, and encouraging self-esteem "in a safe environment for students without penalties for error".
requirements: Questionnaires must be generated per topic and a link distributed to students for after-class completion
constraints: Participation averaged only 42.02% of enrolled students; three questions showed a correct-answer rate under 20%
target_learning_goals: review and consolidation of class concepts; feedback on challenging topics
examples: Brain tumors and traumatic brain injury required two classes each but only one questionnaire per topic
key_sources: Gutiérrez-González R, Zamarron A, Royuela A, Rodriguez-Boto G. (2023). Flipped classroom applied to Neurosurgery in undergraduate medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04158-8

article_title: Supporting Undergraduate Biology Students' Academic Success: Comparing Two Workshop Interventions.
citation: Hensley Lauren, Kulesza Amy, Peri Joshua, Brady Anna C., Wolters Christopher A., Sovic David, Breitenberger Caroline. (2021). Supporting Undergraduate Biology Students' Academic Success: Comparing Two Workshop Interventions. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.21-03-0068
title: Deliver learning-strategy workshops within course structure after an exam, when students are receptive to feedback
description: The article's workshops were held in students' regular lab setting following the results of the first exam, following McGuire's model. The authors state this approach "emphasized the academic rigor of the workshop, communicated the instructor's support for the content, and conveyed information to students when they were receptive to feedback on how they studied." Timing the intervention right after grade feedback makes students receptive to changing study strategies.
requirements: Delivered during regularly scheduled class or lab time so all students can attend
constraints: Interventions were delivered the week following release of first-exam grades in a single introductory biology course
examples: Both workshops were held during required lab sections in week 6, after students received first-exam grades
key_sources: Hensley Lauren, Kulesza Amy, Peri Joshua, Brady Anna C., Wolters Christopher A., Sovic David, Breitenberger Caroline. (2021). Supporting Undergraduate Biology Students' Academic Success: Comparing Two Workshop Interventions. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.21-03-0068

article_title: Using Simulation Training to Promote Nurses' Effective Handling of Workplace Violence: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
citation: Ming Jin-Lain, Huang Hui-Mei, Hung Shiao-Pei, Chang Ching-I, Hsu Yueh-Shuang, Tzeng Yuann-Meei, Huang Hsin-Yi, Hsu Teh-Fu. (2019). Using Simulation Training to Promote Nurses’ Effective Handling of Workplace Violence: A Quasi-Experimental Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16193648
title: Workplace Violence Simulation Training Course
description: A 3-h course for nursing staff combining classroom explanation, a simulation video of verbal and physical violence, demonstration of communication and breakaway skills, and group simulation exercises with scenario review discussion. The course was developed "based on the systematic reviews and nursing staff focus group interviews", and its teaching video followed Jeffries' simulation design principles of introduction, learning objective, case study, and assessment of countermeasures. Participants worked in four groups of eight to nine persons, and two expert focus group interviews examined content validity.
requirements: Nursing staff participants in high-risk units such as emergency departments and medical and surgical wards
Teaching video organized from real situations and expert review of content validity
constraints: Evaluated only in a single-group pre-/post-test design at one medical center, so sustainability of learning effects could not be measured
target_learners: Generalist nurses in high-risk units of a medical center
target_learning_goals: Confidence in coping with patient aggression
examples: The course schedule in Table 1 allots 60 min to reviewing workplace violence prevention, 10 min to the simulation video, 30 min each to verbal-abuse and physical-violence skills, and 50 min to group simulation exercises and discussion

Using Simulation Training to Promote Nurses’ Effective Handling of Workplace Violence: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
